title: Not Drinking Liquor
note: In ruining conduct and understanding, liquor is like the women of the last chapter. This chapter tells the worth of not drinking it, by speaking of what it does.

couplets.plain: Those who live in love with liquor are never feared, and they lose their glory.
couplets.pm: Rulers in love with liquor are never feared by their enemies, and lose even the glory they already had. Without understanding, they aren’t feared even when great in wealth and army. They lose the glory their forebears won because people scorn them. So their rule doesn’t go well.

links.reason: The drinker stops being feared and loses his glory as well.

couplets.plain: Don’t drink liquor. If anyone must, let it be those who don’t care to be counted by the worthy.
couplets.pm: People with understanding should not drink liquor, which takes it away. If some insist on drinking, let it be those who don’t want good people to take note of them. Those who have gained rare understanding and destroy it with liquor aren’t counted even with the animals, which never had it.

couplets.plain: Being drunk is hateful even in your mother’s sight. What must it be in the sight of the worthy?
couplets.pm: Getting drunk is hateful even before your mother, who is glad whatever you do. What then of the worthy, who bear no fault at all? Mind, speech and body are out of your control, so shame is lost, and even she can’t bear it. The worthy know liquor ruins both lives and shun it from afar, so need it be said?
couplets.sensitive: Shames a person with a drinking problem through his mother's disgust

links.quote: hateful even in your mother’s sight

couplets.plain: The good woman called Shame turns her back on those guilty of the great, despised fault called liquor.
couplets.pm: Shame, the noble lady, fears even to look at those with the great fault called liquor, and won’t face them. “Despised” because people shun them from afar, afraid even to see them. “Great” because it can’t be washed away. “Good woman” because she doesn’t stay with the low. Making shame a woman follows Sanskrit usage.

links.quote: the great, despised fault called liquor

couplets.plain: Paying out your wealth to buy senselessness shows you don’t know what to do.
couplets.pm: Someone who pays for liquor to lose himself has, as the cause of this, a not knowing what to do that is the fruit of past deeds. If you don’t know yourself, there is no need to say you know nothing else. People who know don’t pay for something bad, so buying this ignorance must come from an earlier ignorance.

links.quote: Paying out your wealth to buy senselessness
links.reason: Drink goes unnamed, but the trade is plain: wealth paid out for mere senselessness.

links.quote: shows you don’t know what to do
links.reason: Puts the bargain to the drinker in plain terms: wealth out, senselessness back.

couplets.plain: People asleep are no different from the dead. People who drink liquor are always drinking poison.
couplets.pm: The sleeping differ from the dead, yet lacking understanding at the time, they can’t be told apart. So too drinkers and those who take poison, at all times. He rejects the reading that pairs sleepers with poison-takers, who can be revived, and the dead with drinkers, who are given up on. That has no tie to the subject, and the word order won’t bear it.

links.reason: Calls liquor what it is, a dose of poison.
Drinkers are set beside sleepers and the dead.

couplets.plain: Those who drink in secret till their eyes droop will always be laughed at by their townsfolk, who see right through them.
couplets.pm: Those who drink in secret and whose understanding sinks under it are always laughed at by people of their own town, who guess what has gone on inside. They see the drunkenness in the weakness, and from that they know of the drinking.

links.reason: Drinking in hiding ends in the laughter of the townsfolk anyway.

couplets.plain: Give up saying, “I have never been drunk.” What you hid in your heart will only show the more, then and there.
couplets.pm: Having drunk in secret, stop telling people when sober that you have never touched liquor. The moment you drink, the fault you hid in your heart for fear of blame comes out, and greater than before.

links.quote: Give up saying, “I have never been drunk.”

couplets.plain: Reasoning with a drunk is like taking a lamp to look for someone who has dived under water.
couplets.pm: Showing a drunk man reasons why this is wrong is like searching with a lamp for a man who has dived into water. A lamp can’t go under water, and reasons can’t go into his mind.

couplets.plain: When a drinker, sober for the moment, sees a drunk man, doesn’t he think of how he slips when he has drunk?
couplets.pm: When a drinker, sober and not drinking, sees another reeling from drink, it seems he doesn’t think that his own lapse is just like this. Lapse means losing control of mind, speech and body. If he reasoned out the disgrace of it, he would give it up. This is the reason for giving it up.

links.quote: doesn’t he think of how he slips when he has drunk?

ideaLinks.quote: The good woman called Shame turns her back
ideaLinks.reason: Shame turns her back on those with the fault of liquor.
Even glory already won is lost to those in love with liquor.
